title: Trump’s Iran Negotiations: Less Art of the Deal, More Art of Concealing Defeat | Council on Foreign Relations
gist: Elliott Abrams argues that despite Israel largely dismantling Iran's regional 'ring of fire' proxy network and Iran facing serious domestic unrest, Trump's evident eagerness for a deal is weakening the U.S. negotiating position, risking a settlement that hands Iran control of the Strait of Hormuz, saves the regime financially, and drives Gulf allies like Saudi Arabia to seek other protectors.

themes.theme: Iran's proxy network has been dismantled, but the regime itself is also weakening

insights.claim: Hamas's October 7, 2023 attack was the culmination of years of Iranian efforts to encircle Israel using proxies: Hamas and Hezbollah controlling Gaza and Lebanon, Iran-backed Shia militias dominating Iraq, and coordination with the Houthis in Yemen and the Assad regime in Syria.
insights.speaker: Elliott Abrams
insights.so_what: Frames the current conflict as the culmination of a long-running Iranian regional strategy, not an isolated 2026 escalation.
insights.locator: Hamas’s assault on October 7, 2023, was the culmination

insights.claim: Israel has since torn apart Iran's 'ring of fire': Hamas is badly weakened and Israel controls half of Gaza, Hezbollah is disrupted enough that the Lebanese government and army can now contemplate challenging it, the Assad regime fell, and Iraq's government is pushing back against Shia militias.
insights.speaker: Elliott Abrams
insights.so_what: Iran's regional proxy leverage has structurally declined, which is why the outcome of direct U.S.-Iran negotiations now matters even more for regional power balance.
insights.locator: Hamas is badly weakened and Israel has taken control of half of Gaza

insights.claim: Iran also faces domestic weakness: a major uprising earlier this year was put down only through the slaughter of tens of thousands of unarmed civilian protesters, and most Iranians reportedly loathe the theocracy that governs them.
insights.speaker: Elliott Abrams
insights.so_what: Domestic fragility gives the U.S. leverage to press advantage, per the author, rather than rescue the regime through a quick deal.
insights.locator: But Iran’s weakness is also domestic: a dramatic uprising

themes.theme: Trump's deal urgency is undermining U.S. leverage

insights.claim: The Trump administration faces a choice between building on Iran's weakness to further degrade the regime, or accepting a quick accommodation that effectively rescues it, and Trump's evident desire for a deal has weakened his negotiating hand.
insights.speaker: Elliott Abrams
insights.so_what: The core investment-relevant call: whether Iran gets a face-saving deal or continued pressure determines Gulf security risk and oil-market trajectory for the rest of the year.
insights.locator: The question now facing the Trump administration

insights.claim: Continuing the U.S. blockade of Iranian oil exports could batter Iran's economy, but may not deliver results before the U.S. congressional elections in November, and Trump seems unwilling to subordinate political timing to national-security goals the way George W. Bush did with the 2006 Iraq troop surge.
insights.speaker: Elliott Abrams
insights.so_what: Election-driven urgency, not the merits of the blockade, is likely to determine whether U.S. pressure on Iranian oil exports continues or is prematurely relaxed.
insights.locator: Faced with a similar problem in 2006

insights.claim: Trump needs a quick end to the confrontation so oil can flow again and prices drop fast, putting him in the position of a seller who needs cash urgently and cannot hold out for a better price.
insights.speaker: Elliott Abrams
insights.so_what: Trump's own urgency for lower oil prices is itself the leverage Iran is exploiting in negotiations — a dynamic that could push toward a settlement favorable to Tehran.
insights.locator: He wants to end the confrontation with Iran so that oil quickly resumes flowing

themes.theme: What Iran is demanding: control of the Strait of Hormuz

insights.claim: Iran's regime would be financially saved if it can monetize the Strait of Hormuz and freely export its own oil; being seen as having confronted and beaten the United States would strengthen the regime and let it demand tribute from Gulf Arab oil producers.
insights.speaker: Elliott Abrams
insights.so_what: An Iran-favorable Hormuz settlement is not just a regional-security event but a direct threat to Gulf producer autonomy and pricing power over oil flows.
insights.locator: The Iranian regime will be saved financially

insights.claim: If Gulf oil producers can no longer rely on the United States for security, they will instead cut deals with Iran or search for other protectors, as already demonstrated by the new defense pact Saudi Arabia signed with Pakistan and Turkey.
insights.speaker: Elliott Abrams
insights.so_what: Directly links the Iran negotiation outcome to Gulf state hedging behavior, such as the Saudi-Pakistan-Turkey pact — a signal to watch for further Gulf alignment shifts away from Washington.
insights.quote: Gulf oil producers’ reliance on the United States for their security will be replaced by deals with Iran and a search for other protectors, as we have just seen in the new defense pact Saudi Arabia signed with Pakistan and Turkey.
insights.locator: Gulf oil producers’ reliance on the United States

insights.claim: The U.S. Fifth Fleet (NAVCENT), headquartered in Bahrain, has been under missile and drone attack from Iran all year and has suffered severe damage; relocating it and CENTCOM's Qatar headquarters farther from Iran risks effectively ceding the Gulf to Iranian control.
insights.speaker: Elliott Abrams
insights.so_what: Physical degradation of forward U.S. naval presence in the Gulf is a leading indicator of whether Washington can credibly guarantee Gulf shipping security going forward.
insights.quote: That move would quickly turn the Gulf into an Iranian lake, with the United States and its naval warships unable to enter.
insights.locator: This naval element of U.S. Central Command

themes.theme: A pattern of weak deals and inconsistent signaling

insights.claim: The June memorandum of understanding with Iran was a bad deal: it did not clearly state that the Strait of Hormuz is an international waterway open to all nations without tolling, and it legitimized Iran's intrusions into Lebanon's internal affairs, which was mentioned five times in the MOU's first paragraph.
insights.speaker: Elliott Abrams
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence the prior negotiating round already conceded ground on the single most market-relevant issue — free transit through Hormuz.
insights.locator: The memorandum of understanding (MOU) negotiated in June

insights.claim: The Trump administration's response to Iran has swung between threats of total destruction delivered in crude language, followed by no action, then more threats, then more inaction, leaving Americans and U.S. allies unable to judge whether the administration has a bottom line at all.
insights.speaker: Elliott Abrams
insights.so_what: Policy unpredictability itself is emboldening Iran to escalate its demands, per the author — a risk factor for continued volatility in oil markets tied to negotiation headlines.
insights.quote: there has been nothing steady about the administration’s or the president’s reactions. These have included threats of total destruction (delivered with crude and foul language) followed by no action, then more threats, then more inaction.
insights.locator: The MOU contained several unacceptable terms

insights.claim: The current negotiating weakness is a reversal from a year ago: the U.S. position of strength built via Operation Midnight Hammer in June 2025 and subsequent strikes on Iran's nuclear program and Hormuz control is now eroding, emboldening Iran to demand further concessions such as U.S. reparations.
insights.speaker: Elliott Abrams
insights.so_what: The trajectory of leverage is deteriorating, not improving — investors should not assume the U.S. military position from mid-2025 still holds today.
insights.quote: Iran is now seeking even more conditions, such as U.S. reparations, that are obvious nonstarters.
insights.locator: This is a tragic position to be in for an administration

insights.claim: Along with Ukraine negotiations, the Iran talks are the most serious foreign policy test facing the Trump administration, and the outcome will be binary: either Iran ends up controlling the Strait of Hormuz or it does not.
insights.speaker: Elliott Abrams
insights.so_what: Frames Hormuz control as the single clearest binary catalyst to watch for oil-market and Gulf-security repricing.
insights.quote: In the end, the facts will be impossible to paper over with vague language: Iran will either control the Strait of Hormuz or it will not.
insights.locator: Along with potential negotiations over Ukraine

insights.claim: If Iran ends up controlling the Strait of Hormuz, it will have effectively driven the United States out of the Persian Gulf, with major effects on every Gulf state, and will also undermine U.S. security commitments in Asia and Europe by signaling that Washington treats commitments as temporary under the Trump administration through January 2029.
insights.speaker: Elliott Abrams
insights.so_what: A negotiated Iranian win on Hormuz would be read globally as a template for testing U.S. security guarantees elsewhere — relevant to Taiwan and NATO-adjacent risk premia, not just Gulf risk.

insights.locator: Such an outcome will inevitably undermine U.S. commitments
